items.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998
items.q: That playing with Ella and the list of people you’ve played with, Zoot Sims and Sweets Edison, those are great moments

ctx.x: It was actually a very good writer, a guy named Don Specht who was a jazz, a Bud Powell piano player. He could sit down and sound just like Bud Powell. But he, like a lot of guys, he’d gotten into writing jingles and he was good at it, and he always hired the hippest players — he’d have Shelly Manne and Joe Pass or whoever, and doing these kind of idiotic little jingles, but he’d try to make them as good as he could and have good players. So I hadn’t thought of that in years. Something triggered that. But I…

No. Those things are great. And that’s what — people I don’t think have a realistic picture of what jazz musicians, or a lot of musicians, how they really make a living. That playing with Ella and the list of people you’ve played with, Zoot Sims and Sweets Edison, those are great moments, and you’re recording here, but that doesn’t happen every single day.

No. Those are the highlights and high points. But unless you maybe were touring for long periods with a Stan Getz, or — like for instance I worked with Stan in different venues, concert situations, but never to tour, for like six months or whatever. So yeah, you have to fill up the rest of your time with other stuff, and so I’ve done a lot of stuff. I said to somebody recently, I’ve done just about everything except maybe play in a circus band, because they didn’t use keyboards then, now they do. But a lot of it…
